pr_title: Prevent JS interop after circuit disposal. Fixes #32808
pr_body:
See more details about the problem at https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/32808#issuecomment-845236683. In summary, any component that attempts JS interop during disposal (for example, `<Virtualize>`) would hang until the JS call times out, preventing cleanup of any scoped resources for that period.

This PR changes how JS interop works after a circuit has begun disposal (which typically means the user has closed their browser tab or navigated away):

 * Before: JS interop calls would not get any response from the browser, so they'd just hang for a minute and eventually time out with an exception
 * After: JS interop calls will throw immediately using a new exception type (`JSDisconnectedException`)

I think we can regard this as *not* a breaking change because the calls would have eventually thrown anyway, and still do. It now just completes this process faster. The advantages of this change are:

1. DI scopes no longer live for an extra minute before cleanup in this case (e.g., when you have an active `<Virtualize>` component and the user closes the tab). They now clean up immediately.
2. Component authors who want to treat this as not-an-error now have a specific exception type they can catch and suppress. This is now done inside `Virtualize` so it won't even get logged as an error. This makes sense in cases where you were only trying to do JS interop to clean up browser-side state, and obviously don't care about that if the browser is already gone.

If we wanted, we could consider more dramatic options like:

 * **Not treating JS interop calls as failing with exceptions if the browser is disconnected.** I think that's a bad idea because (1) it would be hugely breaking, and (2) semantically it doesn't make sense - we won't know if the developer actually requires some info back from the browser or wants to know for sure whether a void call was received and completed.
 * **Auto-suppressing `JSDisconnectedException` entirely from logs.** I think that's a bad idea because it likely prevents developers from discovering that one was even happening. And then if their disposal logic looked like `DoJsCleanUp(); DoDotNetCleanUp();`, they would not realise that the `DoDotNetCleanUp` part never executes. I think developers need to know this is an error and it's up to them to try/catch if they want to control how it's handled.

> Do we need to do anything for calls that might already be in-flight?

I considered it, but didn't think it was desirable because:

(1) it's not required to solve any known problem (the call will eventually time out anyway, and isn't keeping the circuit open)
(2) it's more likely to affect people with existing code in ways we haven't predicted
(3) it's trickier to implement since we would have to change a bunch of things about how the timeouts get triggered or get surfaced as exceptions

Overall since it's not required to solve the current problem here, I wasn't inclined to expand the scope of the solution. We could do it in the future if a sufficient need arises.

issue_context.title: Blazor virtualize component causes scoped services to never be disposed
issue_context.body:
### Describe the bug
Virtualize component prevents scoped injected services from being disposed.

### To Reproduce
Here is a sample repo:
[BlazorVirtualizeServiceDisposeTest](https://github.com/cristian-recoseanu/BlazorVirtualizeServiceDisposeTest)

The `VirtualizePage` renders multiple `TestComponent` components which depend on the scoped service `ScopedServiceTest`.

Using the `Virtualize` component to render them causes the scoped service to never be disposed when refreshing/closing the page.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/15727528/118624450-155e3a00-b7c1-11eb-99cb-aeb261b2fced.png)

Uncommenting the section using the `Virtualize` component and using a foreach works as indented. The scoped service is created and always disposed correctly.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/15727528/118624704-48a0c900-b7c1-11eb-999d-b89e6b63f8ee.png)

comments: @SteveSandersonMS can you please look into this? If turns out to be true, we can bring this in for preview5 potentially.

Thanks for reporting this, @cristian-recoseanu! From investigations, it looks to me like those scoped services *will* eventually be disposed, but a problematic aspect of the implementation means it will take 1 minute before that happens.

### Investigation

Looks like a real issue, which comes down to two things:

1. The `IAsyncDisposable` implementation inside `Renderer` relies on the wholesome idea that all components will complete their disposal quickly: https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/659e492495884d37cde5a567f3c73b0550c561e5/src/Components/Components/src/RenderTree/Renderer.cs#L913-L914
    While it might be OK to let components take a long time to dispose while the circuit remains active, as soon as the circuit is being shut down, we shouldn't let them take as long as they want and pin resources in memory until they eventually finish (or maybe never eventually finish).
2. The behavior of `RemoteJSRuntime` when a circuit is disconnected isn't great. Any subsequent async JS interop calls will be issued as if the circuit was still there, but of course there will never be a reply, so they just hang until they finally time out (default: 1 minute).
 
Since `<Virtualize>` tries to clean things up on the JS side when being disposed, those two things above combine to make it take 1 minute to complete its `IAsyncDisposable` task, and the DI container remains undisposed until then.

I don't think this is a defect in `<Virtualize>`. In general we should expect components to try doing JS interop calls as part of async disposal. Instead, I think we need to make sure that either (1) JS interop calls fails immediately if/when the circuit is disconnected, or (2) that the `Renderer's` async disposal path doesn't actually wait for components' async disposal paths. Maybe we should even do both of these, since each of them alone still seems to leave open edge cases where things would be left hanging longer than you want.

@dotnet/aspnet-blazor-eng - opinions on whether it's either, both, or something else?

In case it might be relevant, with https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/32849 is there some changes we should make in the Renderer code (or in any other areas) with the new AsyncServiceScope in that PR?

I'm don't think `AsyncServiceScope` will change this. The renderer disposal process hangs *before* we ask the DI scope to be disposed, because the component hierarchy disposal runs first and doesn't complete.

The question we need to answer first is whether there should be an exception if you try to do JS interop calls during `IAsyncDispose` after the circuit is gone. On one hand it should be an exception because the call couldn't complete, and you told us to await it. On the other hand, this will *always* happen whenever the user closes a tab, so this is very noisy in server logs. 

But even then we still have a problem either way. Given that you have code like `await JS.InvokeAsync("someCleanupLogic")`, we can't continue with the rest of your component's disposal logic after this, whether or not it throws. So JS interop during async disposal might leave other things undisposed. We would have to recommend that all use of JS interop during disposal be fire-and-forget (e.g., `_ = JS.InvokeVoidAsync("someCleanupLogic")` - this will still log an exception but won't prevent other disposal logic from running.

I suppose the right answer is that `JS.InvokeAsync` should throw as noisily as possible if the browser already disconnected. Yes, that will be noisy in logs, which is precisely what might help developers discover they need to do something about it (e.g., try/catch for the specific JS exception that occurs).

Thanks for looking at this @SteveSandersonMS! It hadn't crossed my mind to wait for a timeout. Empirical evidence pointed at the Virtualize component being the culprit but as your investigation points out this is a much more deeper issue in the framework.

> 
> 
> I suppose the right answer is that `JS.InvokeAsync` should throw as noisily as possible if the browser already disconnected. Yes, that will be noisy in logs, which is precisely what might help developers discover they need to do something about it (e.g., try/catch for the specific JS exception that occurs).

I think this is a good approach which increases visibility of the problems so developers can cater for them in their implementations.

review_comments: We aren't concerned about a potential race condition between this func and https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/32901/files#diff-7fac6aa482260bd9b68de9fd59db0da9d8532c59ecdfd4468c0f51d371b562aaR82 because we assume a single thread, correct?
Great question, and yes, we absolutely expect code invoking the JS runtime to be on the circuit sync context, so only one at a time.
Minor: Do we have a convention to have `else` always? I would simply not have it and throw.

In cases where the `if`/`else` clauses could be written equally in either order (like this one), I usually prefer to have the `else` explicitly so as to make the two halves of more equal status to each other. I think it more closely matches how people speak in natural language when talking about two alternatives. For example a person might say "*if it's sunny go to the park, otherwise go to the museum*", whereas they wouldn't say "*if it's sunny go to the park and ignore anything else I say. Go to the museum.*"

I normally prefer to skip the `else` in cases where the `if` part plays the role of a guard clause, where it's natural to terminate the flow if the guard clause applies. This is more like "*Customers under 18 are not permitted. We hereby give 1 token to each customer.*"

Of course it's all subjective and there isn't really a ground truth here. Based on preference I propose to leave it, but if this is really troubling to anyone, I'll change it!

```suggestion
                    throw new JSDisconnectedException(
                        "JavaScript interop calls cannot be issued at this time. This is because the circuit has disconnected " +
                        "and is being disposed.");
```
